questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a trust boundary actually runs
questions.learningObjective: Locate a trust boundary by data custody rather than network position
questions.stem: Explain where the trust boundary lies in a clinic system that receives referral text from a partner practice's portal and stores it in the patient's record.

answer.exemplar: Networks are drawn in terms of cables and addresses, and it is tempting to put trust boundaries where the lines are, so that everything inside the clinic's building is trusted and everything outside is not. That drawing is misleading for a clinic system. The referral arrives over the same internal network as the staff directory and the pathology feed, yet it is the least trustworthy of the three, because it was written by another organisation and was never under the clinic's control. The real boundary is the moment the referral stops being the partner's document and becomes the clinic's record. On one side of that moment the clinic has no responsibility for the content; on the other side the clinic is storing it, displaying it to staff, and possibly acting on it. That is where the clinic has to decide what shape the referral must have, how to validate it, and what to do when it does not fit. A boundary drawn around the building would hide exactly the decision that needed attention.

questions.explanation: The boundary lies where the referral stops being the partner's document and becomes the clinic's data, where the clinic decides what to accept and validate. It is not the network link.
questions.hint: Ask where the data changes hands.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order a threat model is built in
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of modelling order on coverage
questions.stem: Explain to a clinic manager why the order in which a threat model is built matters, using the booking system as the example.

answer.exemplar: Threat models go wrong in a predictable way: they are built in an order that flatters the conclusion the writer already wants. If a clinic starts by listing the threats it is worried about, those worries will anchor everything afterwards, and whole parts of the system will go unexamined because no worry happened to point at them. If it starts by choosing controls, the model becomes a justification for the control it already bought. The disciplined order is data first, then flow, then entry point, then threat, then control. Data because the thing being protected defines what matters; flow because a record that never moves is exposed in a completely different way from one that crosses eleven boundaries; entry point because that is where the system's assumptions about the world stop holding; threat because a threat is a story about something happening at a named point; and only then control, chosen because it addresses that particular story rather than because it was in the plan already.

questions.explanation: The order decides what the model covers. If data flows are mapped first, later questions have a place to sit, and if entry points come next, threats attach to real points.
questions.hint: Ask what a wrong order leaves out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which of the two filters fails open
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of a filter failing open
questions.stem: Explain what it means for a clinic filter to fail open, and why the label matters when reading a design.

answer.exemplar: The phrase describes what a filter does when it meets something it has no rule for. A referral filter that has a rule for every shape it expects, and a deny rule for everything else, is closed: anything it cannot place is refused. A filter that permits anything it cannot classify is open: a new message format from a partner practice, a stray character in a clinician code, or an internal error while parsing all result in the referral being accepted. The difference matters more than the list of rules, because the unrecognised cases are the ones nobody tested. In a clinic, an open filter in front of referral text means that text the clinic has never seen can end up in a patient record and on a clinician's screen without anyone having decided to allow it. A closed filter at the same point means the referral is refused and a human looks at why, which is slower and far easier to reason about.

questions.explanation: Failing open means that when the filter cannot decide it lets the input through, so an odd format becomes accepted data. The label matters because it describes the cases nobody thought about.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to input the filter cannot judge.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a rule is checked in two places
questions.learningObjective: Explain why both an edge check and a domain check are needed
questions.stem: Explain why a clinic checks both the shape of a referral and the clinical rule about it, rather than relying on one of the two.

answer.exemplar: The two checks answer two different questions and a referral has to survive both. The shape check asks whether this is a referral message at all: is it the agreed format, does it carry the fields the integration expects, is every value the right kind of thing. This check belongs at the edge because it can be performed on everything cheaply, before any work is done, and because it stops malformed input from ever reaching the service that would have to interpret it. The clinical check asks whether this referral makes sense for this patient in this clinic: does the named clinician exist and still work here, has this patient already been discharged, is the referral for a service the patient is actually registered with. This check cannot live at the edge, because answering it requires the clinic's own records, and it is the one that catches the dangerous case, a message that is perfectly well formed and refers to something impossible. A clinic that only checks shape will accept the impossible referral; a clinic that only checks clinical rules will spend its time and its error handling on malformed rubbish.

questions.explanation: The shape check catches input that is not a referral, so the service never interprets rubbish, and it is cheap at the edge. The clinical check catches a well-formed referral that cannot be acted on.
questions.hint: Ask what each check can see that the other cannot.

questions.topic: Trust follows the origin of a value, not the network it arrived on
questions.learningObjective: Explain why origin governs trust rather than network path
questions.stem: Explain why a clinic should judge a value by where it came from rather than by the network it arrived over.

answer.exemplar: It is tempting to treat the internal network as the safe place and everything beyond it as suspect, because that is how the diagram is drawn and because it maps neatly onto how people talk about systems. A clinic that adopts that habit draws the wrong conclusion about the values it handles. The referral from a partner practice travels along the same internal network as the laboratory result, yet the result is generated by an instrument the clinic owns, calibrates and maintains, while the referral is a document written by a stranger at another organisation and never under the clinic's control. Neither the shared path nor the identical addresses tell you which of the two to trust. The judgement has to be made about the producer: an instrument inside the clinic that the clinic can vouch for, and a third party's document that has to be validated on its own terms before it is allowed anywhere near a patient record. If the rule is instead inside is fine, the clinic has quietly agreed to trust every partner's referral, every expired result file and every misconfigured device that shares the cable.

questions.explanation: Networks say where a packet was, not who wrote what is inside it, and the internal network carries both the clinic's laboratory results and a partner's referrals. Trust must attach to the producer, not the wire.
questions.hint: Ask who produced the value, not where it sat.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which of the two filters fails open
questions.learningObjective: Contrast open and closed filter behaviour
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a filter that fails open and one that fails closed, and why a clinic has to choose deliberately.

answer.exemplar: Every filter is a decision procedure, and the interesting question is not only what it does with input it recognises but what it does with input it does not. A filter that admits what it cannot classify is open; a filter that refuses it is closed. In a clinic the two produce very different outcomes for the same unexpected referral. Open, the unexpected referral becomes part of a patient record, is shown to a clinician, and may be acted on, and nobody was consulted because the system behaved as designed. Closed, the referral is refused, the sender is told, and a person investigates, which costs time but keeps a human in the loop precisely where the model was incomplete. The choice should be made deliberately, because the default is whatever the framework or the author chose, and defaults are often chosen for convenience. It is also worth noting that a filter can be open in one direction and closed in another, so the two labels describe a behaviour to be checked rather than a property to be assumed.

questions.explanation: A filter that fails open admits what it cannot classify, while one that fails closed refuses it. The choice matters because the cases it cannot handle are the ones nobody tested.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to input the filter cannot classify.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why entry points come before threats
questions.learningObjective: Explain why threats need entry points to be actionable
questions.stem: Explain why a clinic that identifies threats before entry points ends up with a model that cannot be checked.

answer.exemplar: The entry point list is the index of a threat model, and without it the document is a collection of anxieties. Consider the difference between two sentences: someone might modify a referral, and someone might modify a referral in the partner portal integration before it is written into the patient record. The first cannot be acted on, tested, assigned to an owner or retested after a fix. It does not say which component to look at, which log to read, whether the problem has already happened or what evidence would show that it has. The second names a place, and everything else follows from that: the component can be reviewed, the boundary where the text enters can be found, the threat can be checked against the controls already in place, and a fix can be verified later. This is why experienced modellers are reluctant to write threats early. The worries are usually right, and writing them down feels like progress, but a worry without an address cannot be tracked, so it quietly never gets addressed. The entry point list turns a list of worries into a work list.

questions.explanation: A threat only says something when attached to a place where data enters the system, so worries without entry points cannot be traced to the design, tested or assigned. The entry points give each worry an address.
questions.hint: Ask where each worry would be looked for.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which of the two filters fails open
questions.learningObjective: Argue a filter's failure direction from its purpose
questions.stem: Describe how a clinic should decide whether a filter on incoming clinical data should fail open or fail closed.

answer.exemplar: There is no answer that is right for every filter, so the decision has to be argued rather than assumed. The question to ask is what the filter is for. Where the filter is the last thing standing between a value and an action that must not happen on bad information, such as a discharge decision or an automated dosing rule, closing is the only defensible behaviour, because the cost of refusing an unrecognised value is a delay that a person can look at while the cost of admitting it is harm that cannot be undone. Where the filter only sorts material for a person who will review it anyway, opening is reasonable, since the review catches what the filter misses and the delay of a refusal buys nothing. The two failure modes are not symmetric, though: with an open filter the failure is silent, and the unrecognised case is precisely the one nobody wrote a rule for. A clinic that chooses open should therefore make sure the review step exists and that someone is watching it, otherwise the choice is merely a way of avoiding the decision.

questions.explanation: The decision turns on the filter's purpose. If it protects against a value that must never be acted on, closing is safer, since an unrecognised value causes delay rather than harm. If it routes data for review, opening is cheaper.
questions.hint: Ask what happens downstream when the filter is wrong.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A domain invariant rather than a request rule
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a request rule from a rule over clinic state
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a rule about what a request must contain and a rule about what may be true in the clinic's records.

answer.exemplar: The two kinds of rule look similar on the page and behave completely differently in the system. A request rule is a statement about the message: this field must be present, this must be a date in that format, this must be within the allowed length. It can be checked by looking at the message and nothing else, which is why it can be enforced by a generic filter sitting at the edge of the system and reused for every kind of message that arrives. A rule about the clinic's records is a statement about the world: this patient is not discharged, this appointment type is one we currently offer, this clinician is on the rota today. None of that is visible in the message, so such a rule can only be checked against the state the clinic holds, and it must be checked at the moment the action would take effect. The practical difference is where each rule lives and what it needs. The edge filter protects the system from inputs it cannot handle, and the domain check protects the clinic from actions that make no sense in the light of what it already knows, and only the second of those can say anything about the world rather than about the form of the request.

questions.explanation: A request rule is about the message, so it can be checked from the message alone. A domain invariant is about the records, so it must be checked against current state and holds however the message is formed.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule is checked against.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why entry points come before threats
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a listed entry point from an analysed one

stimulus.body: Clinic note, review meeting. The team recorded four entry points: the booking form, the referral feed, the laboratory instrument feed and the staff roster import. Threats were raised against the booking form and the referral feed. When asked about the instrument feed, the laboratory lead explained that results from the clinic's own instruments are written directly into the record store and never pass through a service that a person or an outside system can reach.

questions.stem: What does this note suggest about the model so far?

options.text: The model is complete, because the instrument feed carries no untrusted input
options.misconception: treats the absence of threats as proof of no risk

options.text: The instrument feed has been listed but not analysed, because no threats were raised against it yet
The instrument feed should be removed from the list, because it is not a real entry point
options.misconception: deletes an entry point instead of analysing it

options.text: The laboratory lead's explanation means the instrument feed needs no threat, since results are clinic-generated
options.misconception: takes an assurance as an exemption

questions.explanation: Listing an entry point and analysing it are separate acts, and the instrument feed was listed but no threat was raised against it, so that part of the model is untouched, not proven safe. The tempting answers treat silence as evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what was actually done with that entry point.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A domain invariant rather than a request rule
questions.learningObjective: Place a domain rule where the state it depends on lives
questions.stem: A clinic wants to enforce that a prescription cannot be issued to a patient marked as discharged. First, state where that rule belongs; second, state why it cannot live only at the request boundary.

options.text: At the request boundary, because everything must be validated before it enters the system
options.misconception: puts a domain rule at the edge

options.text: In the referral service, because that is where the clinic's records are consulted
options.misconception: places the rule in the wrong service

options.text: At the request boundary and in the referral service, because two copies of a rule are always better
options.misconception: justifies duplication without a reason

options.text: In the prescribing service, because the boundary cannot know the patient's current state

questions.explanation: The rule is about clinic records, so it must be checked where the prescription is created against the current state, and enforced again at the boundary because the boundary protects the service. The tempting answers put a domain rule at the edge.
questions.hint: Ask which party knows the patient's current state.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order a threat model is built in
questions.learningObjective: Explain the coverage blind spot of starting from threats
questions.stem: A clinic's analyst lists threats first, then works out which system parts they touch. What is the main weakness of that order?

options.text: It takes too long, because threat lists are slow to produce
options.misconception: treats the problem as one of effort rather than coverage

options.text: It duplicates work, because the same threat will appear on several systems
options.misconception: invents a duplication cost as the main flaw

options.text: It anchors on the worries, so parts of the system that no worry pointed at are never examined
It produces too many threats, because each worry expands into several entries
options.misconception: treats the problem as one of volume rather than coverage

questions.explanation: Starting from worries means the analysis inherits their blind spots, and any part of the system none of them touched receives no scrutiny. The tempting answers frame the flaw as effort, duplication or volume.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the parts nobody worried about.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which of the two filters fails open
questions.learningObjective: Compare two filters by their behaviour on unclassified input
questions.stem: Two filters are under review at the clinic. Filter A refuses every input it cannot classify, while Filter B admits every one of them. In a month, Filter A refused 300 inputs and Filter B admitted 40. Which statement about the two filters is supported?

options.text: Filter A fails closed and Filter B fails open, so the two handle unclassified input in opposite ways
Filter A fails open and Filter B fails closed, because the counts show which direction each took
options.misconception: reads the refusal count as failing open

options.text: Both filters fail open, because both of them handled input that arrived outside the expected shape
options.misconception: treats handling unknown input as failing open

options.text: Both filters fail closed, because both of them produced a decision on every input
options.misconception: treats producing a decision as failing closed

questions.explanation: A filter that refuses what it cannot classify fails closed, one that admits it fails open, and A refused 300 such inputs while B admitted 40. The tempting answers invert the labels or read direction from counts.
questions.hint: Ask what each filter did with what it could not classify.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Choosing the direction of a filter that can be enumerated
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a growing set affects the filter choice
questions.stem: Explain how the choice between an allowlist and a denylist should change when the set of items a filter must handle grows over time.

answer.exemplar: The direction of a filter is a bet about the future, and the bet has to be made explicitly. An allowlist is the strong promise: everything the system accepts was looked at and approved by somebody. That promise has a cost, because the world does not stand still. Every new appointment type, every new laboratory assay, every new referring department is something the allowlist has not seen, and the filter will refuse it, correctly according to its own rules but awkwardly for the people who are trying to do their jobs. The symptom is not a security event, it is a queue of support tickets asking why a legitimate request was rejected, and each of those tickets is really a request to update the list. A denylist makes the opposite promise: everything is allowed unless somebody has decided it is not. That promise holds up better while the set of legitimate items is still growing, and it needs attention only when a genuinely unacceptable item appears. The choice therefore depends on whether the acceptable set can be exhausted and held still, not on which approach sounds more careful in principle.

questions.explanation: An allowlist promises that everything accepted was considered in advance, and it silently refuses new legitimate items as the world moves, showing up as a support ticket. A denylist accepts new items.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when a new legitimate item appears.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Trust follows the origin of a value, not the network it arrived on
questions.learningObjective: Count traffic kinds by external origin on a shared network
questions.stem: A clinic's internal network carries four kinds of traffic, namely bookings, laboratory results, referrals and roster synchronisation. Laboratory results are produced by the clinic's own instruments and referrals arrive from an external practice. How many of the four kinds originate from a party outside the clinic?
questions.explanation: Of the four kinds, only referrals arrive from an outside party, so the count is 1 even though all four travel on one network. The tempting answers assume the network decides origin or that internal traffic is trusted.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A domain invariant rather than a request rule
questions.learningObjective: Classify a rule that depends on clinic records

stimulus.body: Clinic note. The referral service accepts a document only if it carries a clinician code that appears in the current staff directory, and the document's own signature verifies that it was written by the sending practice. A referral naming a clinician who has left the clinic therefore fails, and a referral signed by an unknown practice is also refused.

questions.stem: What kind of rule does the clinician code requirement express?

options.text: A request rule, because it concerns a field that appears in the incoming document
options.misconception: reads a domain condition as a request rule

options.text: A domain invariant, because it depends on the clinic's directory rather than on the message
An access rule, because it limits who may send a referral into the clinic
options.misconception: confuses a domain condition with a permission check

options.text: A network rule, because the clinician directory is refreshed overnight by a sync job
options.misconception: grounds a domain condition in a transport detail

questions.explanation: The requirement is that the named clinician exists in the clinic's directory, a statement about clinic records rather than the document, so it is a domain invariant and a message can be well formed without it. The tempting answers call it a request rule or a permission check.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule depends on.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a rule is checked in two places
questions.learningObjective: State the distinct coverage of an edge check and a core check
questions.stem: A clinic's referral service validates message structure at its edge and checks clinician codes against the staff directory in its core. First, state what the edge check covers that the core check does not; second, state what the core check covers that the edge check cannot.

options.text: The edge check covers the shape of the message, and the core check covers who may send referrals
options.misconception: confuses the core check with a permission check

options.text: The edge check covers the signature of the sender, and the core check covers whether the message is well formed
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the two checks

options.text: The edge check covers the shape of the message, and the core check covers whether the named clinician exists
The edge check covers who may send referrals, and the core check covers how long the referral stays valid
options.misconception: assigns both checks unrelated properties

questions.explanation: The edge check works from the message alone, so it can judge the shape of a referral, while the core check consults the directory, so it can tell whether the named clinician still works there. The tempting answers swap the roles.
questions.hint: Ask what each check can see.
